cards.back: The boundary that holds Entra ID, licenses, Teams policies, and verified domains for one organization. Why it matters: An SBC paired in the wrong tenant is a different phone system.

cards.front: How do you approach Microsoft 365 tenant?
cards.back: Confirm the tenant before you run Connect-MicrosoftTeams. If it fails: Two engineers edit two tenants and each thinks the other broke the trunk.
A domain added and proven in the tenant. Direct Routing SBC FQDNs must live on one of these domains. Why it matters: onmicrosoft.com cannot carry the SBC name.

cards.front: How do you approach Verified domain?
cards.back: Add the domain, including a sip subdomain, before you pair the gateway. If it fails: Pairing fails because sbc.contoso.com was never verified.
The default tenant domain. It is not a supported domain for a Direct Routing SBC FQDN. Why it matters: People try it because it already resolves inside Microsoft 365.

cards.front: How do you approach onmicrosoft.com domain?
cards.back: Use a domain you verified, such as contoso.com. If it fails: The gateway object is rejected or never becomes healthy.

Direct Routing users must be homed in Microsoft 365, not left on a Skype for Business on-premises registrar. Why it matters: A user who looks licensed and still is not online will not use the online voice route.

cards.front: How do you approach Homed online?
cards.back: Check the user’s registrar before you assign a voice routing policy. If it fails: The policy is assigned and the call never leaves the legacy system.
A coexistence mode. Direct Routing is not supported for users in Islands mode. Why it matters: It is a hard stop, not a tuning problem.

cards.front: How do you approach Islands mode?
cards.back: Move the user to a supported mode before you test PSTN. If it fails: PSTN fails only for the Islands users and nowhere else.
The identity directory for the tenant. Teams users, resource accounts, and admin roles are Entra objects. Why it matters: Voice licenses attach to these objects.

cards.front: How do you approach Entra ID?
cards.back: Create the user or resource account here, then license it, then grant policies. If it fails: A resource account exists in Teams and has no license because nobody looked in Entra.
A disabled-for-sign-in Entra account that represents an auto attendant or a call queue. It is not a human login. Why it matters: The published number is often this account, not a person.

cards.front: How do you approach Resource account?
cards.back: Create it with a Teams admin role and the User Administrator role. If it fails: Agents try to sign in as the queue and the sign-in is correctly blocked.
The Teams voicemail service. It deposits messages in the user’s Exchange mailbox. Why it matters: No mailbox means no voicemail, even when the call routed.

cards.front: How do you approach Cloud Voicemail?
cards.back: Confirm the mailbox and the voicemail policy before you debug the SBC. If it fails: Callers hear a greeting failure and the SBC trace is clean.

The license capability that lets a user use Teams as a phone system. It is not, by itself, a PSTN carrier. Why it matters: People say Phone System, Calling Plan, and Teams Premium as if they were one SKU.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Phone?
cards.back: Assign Teams Phone, then add a connectivity option. If it fails: Outbound PSTN fails because only Teams, not Teams Phone, is assigned.

A Microsoft-operated PSTN option. Domestic, international, and pay-as-you-go are the usual flavors. It is an extra license on top of Teams Phone. Why it matters: E5 may include the phone-system capability and still not include a Calling Plan.

cards.front: How do you approach Calling Plan?
cards.back: Buy the plan only where Microsoft sells it, and assign it to the user. If it fails: A user in an unsupported country is given a Calling Plan SKU that cannot be used.
The license that provides dial-in numbers for meetings. It is not Teams Phone. Why it matters: Without it, outbound conference calls can route through Direct Routing.

cards.front: How do you approach Audio Conferencing?
cards.back: Assign it to people who must publish a dial-in number. If it fails: Conference dial-out hits the SBC and the carrier bill surprises finance.
An add-on for advanced meetings and related features. It does not replace Teams Phone or a Calling Plan. Why it matters: Interview traps treat it as the PSTN license.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Premium?
cards.back: Buy it only for the meeting features you actually need. If it fails: A design removes Calling Plans because Premium was purchased.

The license each auto attendant or call queue resource account needs, even when the account has no phone number. Subscriptions with Teams Phone include a zero-cost allotment you still have to acquire. Why it matters: Do not put Teams Phone Standard on a resource account.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Phone Resource Account license?
cards.back: Assign this license. If you swap off Teams Phone Standard, remove and add in the same license change. If it fails: Queues die after a two-step license swap.

A Calling Plan billed on use. Also the funding pattern, with communications credits, for some voice-app outbound calls. Why it matters: External transfers from a queue are not free just because users have Direct Routing.

cards.front: How do you approach Pay-as-you-go Calling Plan?
cards.back: Fund the resource account when the attendant or queue sends calls to an external number, uses callback, or places on-behalf calls. If it fails: Overflow to a mobile number fails and the user Calling Plan is blamed.
A balance used when a call is not covered by a Calling Plan minute. Voice apps use it for some outbound cases. Why it matters: An empty balance looks like a routing failure.

cards.front: How do you approach Communications credits?
cards.back: Fund the balance and assign it where the prerequisite article requires it. If it fails: The queue worked in the pilot week and stopped when the credit ran out.

A pattern where users place outbound PSTN calls through a resource account’s number instead of each having a number. Why it matters: It is not a free substitute for every Calling Plan scenario. The shared number has its own license rules.

cards.front: How do you approach Shared Calling?
cards.back: Read the current shared-calling prerequisites before you promise it to a site. If it fails: Every user was left numberless and the resource account was never funded.
A shared handset. On Direct Routing it does not need a Calling Plan license. Why it matters: People copy a user bundle onto a hallway phone.

cards.front: How do you approach Common area phone?
cards.back: License the device for Teams and the phone scenario you chose, then assign the number. If it fails: A Calling Plan was purchased for every corridor phone on a Direct Routing design.

Rooms use their own SKU family, not a borrowed user Calling Plan. Names such as Basic and Pro change. Check the current name. Why it matters: A room that cannot join is often a license or a resource account, not a codec.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Rooms license?
cards.back: Assign the current room license to the room account and keep Conditional Access from blocking the device. If it fails: The room account has a user E5 stack and still fails sign-in policy.
Entra policy that can block a phone or a room that is not in the trusted device set. Why it matters: Voice engineers see a SIP 200 and a device that never registers.

cards.front: How do you approach Conditional Access?
cards.back: Exclude or scope device sign-in on purpose. Do not turn Conditional Access off as a test you leave in place. If it fails: Rooms fail on Monday after a security change nobody told voice about.
Microsoft’s network guidance prefers a short path to the Microsoft network, without a proxy in the media path. Why it matters: A proxy that was fine for web traffic adds jitter to RTP.

cards.front: How do you approach Shortest media path?
cards.back: Egress Teams media locally. Do not hairpin a branch through a distant data center unless you mean to. If it fails: One city’s CQD is poor and the firewall team finds a proxy.

Microsoft recommends that you avoid sending real-time Teams media through a VPN. QoS on the VPN does not fix the extra delay. Why it matters: Split-tunnel designs exist so media can go direct while other traffic stays on the VPN.

cards.front: How do you approach VPN and real-time media?
cards.back: Test a call on the VPN and off it before you blame the carrier. If it fails: Every remote user shows high RTT and the office does not.

Teams does not require ExpressRoute. Local internet egress is the usual design. If you do use ExpressRoute, follow the current network article rather than assuming media is happier there. Why it matters: A contract for ExpressRoute is not a QoS design.

cards.front: How do you approach ExpressRoute is optional?
cards.back: Decide the path, then mark DSCP on the path you actually use. If it fails: Media was forced onto a long private path and RTT jumped.

The Teams admin center setting that allows clients to insert DSCP. Without it, a correct ACL still sees unmarked client traffic from managed endpoints that honor the policy. Why it matters: Mac and mobile hard-code some marks. Windows follows policy.

cards.front: How do you approach QoS markers enabled?
cards.back: Turn the insert-markers setting on, then verify at the WAN edge. If it fails: The network is marked and the clients were never told to mark.

Microsoft’s planning note: keep the client-to-network-edge path short, on the order of three to five hops, and the ISP-to-Microsoft edge short as well. Why it matters: Each extra hop is a place a mark can be stripped.

cards.front: How do you approach Three to five hops?
cards.back: Draw the path before you buy bandwidth. If it fails: A branch hairpins through HQ and then out, adding hops and delay.
G.711 at 20 ms is 160 bytes of payload plus 40 bytes of IP, UDP, and RTP. That is 80 kbit/s per direction. Why it matters: People quote 64 kbit/s and under-size the link.

cards.front: How do you approach Layer-3 G.711?
cards.back: Multiply by concurrent calls and by two directions when both ways are busy. If it fails: Thirty calls were planned at 64 kbit/s and the link saturated.
Add an 18-byte Ethernet header to the G.711 20 ms packet and the figure is 87.2 kbit/s per direction. Why it matters: WAN sizing that stops at layer 3 is already short on a LAN you police.

cards.front: How do you approach Ethernet G.711?
cards.back: Use 87.2 kbit/s when the policer sees Ethernet. If it fails: The policer drops the header you forgot.

A certified carrier manages PSTN for you inside the tenant. You need Teams Phone. You do not need a Microsoft Calling Plan or your own SBC. Why it matters: It is the low-operations option when your carrier is in the program.

cards.front: How do you approach Operator Connect?
cards.back: Enable the operator in the admin center and assign the numbers they provide. If it fails: Someone also builds a Direct Routing SBC for the same numbers and the routes fight.

The India-specific operator model. It exists because India PSTN rules are not the same as a generic Operator Connect deployment. Why it matters: A global design that ignores it will fail a regulatory review.

cards.front: How do you approach Operator Connect for India?
cards.back: Use the current India plan article and the licensed operator there. If it fails: A UK SBC was proposed as the egress for an India office.
The user’s mobile SIM number is also their Teams number, through a certified mobile operator. Teams Phone is required. Why it matters: It fits frontline and mobile workers, not a reception queue.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Phone Mobile?
cards.back: Assign the operator number to the user. Do not also treat it as a spare Calling Plan. If it fails: One human has two different caller IDs and the CRM matches neither.

You connect a certified SBC to Teams and bring your own carrier. Users need Teams and Teams Phone. They must be homed online. Islands mode is not supported. Why it matters: This is the option when you still own trunks, a PBX, analog, or a contact-center SBC.

cards.front: How do you approach Direct Routing?
cards.back: Pair the FQDN, open 5061, allow media ranges, assign a voice route. If it fails: The SBC is up and the user has no voice routing policy.

One tenant may use Calling Plans, Operator Connect, Teams Phone Mobile, and Direct Routing at the same time for different users. Why it matters: A global voice policy that assumes one carrier will misroute someone.

cards.front: How do you approach Mixing PSTN options?
cards.back: Give each population a policy that matches its carrier. If it fails: A mobile user matches a Direct Routing route and hairpins.

For commercial Microsoft 365, signal to sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com, then sip2, then sip3, on TCP 5061. GCC High and DoD use different names. Why it matters: DNS can return one address. The firewall must allow the published ranges, not that one answer.

cards.front: How do you approach SIP proxies?
cards.back: Allow 52.112.0.0/14 and 52.120.0.0/14 as published on the plan page, and re-check the page when you change firewalls. If it fails: A lockdown allows only today’s DNS answer and the trunk fails next week.

UDP 3478–3481 and 49152–53247 between the SBC and the media processors, unless media bypass keeps the media off that path. Why it matters: People open 5061 and forget media, so signaling works and audio does not.

cards.front: How do you approach Media ports for Direct Routing?
cards.back: Budget at least two media ports per concurrent call on the SBC. If it fails: Calls connect and both sides hear silence.

Microsoft does not support changing the media target in the middle of an active Direct Routing call. Why it matters: A clever SBC feature that moves media mid-call will not be a supported troubleshooting step.

cards.front: How do you approach Media re-targeting?
cards.back: Negotiate media at setup and leave it. If it fails: Audio dies when a transfer tries to move the RTP peer.
Microsoft’s planning tip: allocate at least two media ports on the SBC for each concurrent call. Why it matters: Port exhaustion looks like random one-way audio.

cards.front: How do you approach Two media ports per call?
cards.back: Size the SBC media range from the busy-hour call count. If it fails: The 51st call connects with no audio.
The dial plan rewrites what a person dialed into a number the routes can match, usually E.164. The first matching rule wins. Why it matters: A route for +44 will never see 020.
Put the specific rules above the general ones. If it fails: A catch-all rule is first, so the emergency rule never runs.

A set of normalization rules you assign to users. A user can have a more specific plan than the tenant default. Why it matters: Two sites that dial local numbers differently need two plans, not one heroic route.

cards.front: How do you approach Tenant dial plan?
cards.back: Grant the plan to the user and test from that user. If it fails: You edit the global plan and a branch with its own plan does not change.

A name that links a voice routing policy to one or more voice routes. The policy’s ordered list of usages is the permission to place those calls. Why it matters: Usages are how you let one site call internationally and another not.

cards.front: How do you approach PSTN usage?
cards.back: Create the usage, attach routes, then put the usage on the policy in the right order. If it fails: International works because the international usage was left on a branch policy.

A number pattern plus an ordered list of SBC gateways. It does nothing until a PSTN usage on the user’s policy points at it. Why it matters: The pattern is a regular expression, not a CUCM route-pattern wildcard.

cards.front: How do you approach Voice route?
cards.back: Anchor the pattern. Test with the normalized number, not the raw digits. If it fails: The route expects 10 digits and the dial plan already added +1.
The per-user list of PSTN usages, in order. Teams walks that order when it looks for a route. Why it matters: Granting the wrong policy is the most common ‘the SBC is broken’ ticket.

cards.front: How do you approach Voice routing policy?
cards.back: Grant it to a test user and read it back with Get-CsOnlineUser. If it fails: The pilot user is still on the global policy, which has no usages.

Each voice route lists SBCs with a priority. Lower priority number is tried first in this campus’s teaching model. Confirm the current article before you depend on a tie. Why it matters: Failover is a list, not a wish.

cards.front: How do you approach Gateway priority?
cards.back: Put the local SBC first and a remote SBC second, then pull the cable in a maintenance window. If it fails: Both gateways are priority 1 and nobody knows which one took the call.
999, 112, and 911 must be normalized on purpose. A general rule that runs first can swallow them. Why it matters: An emergency call that matches an international route is a design defect.

cards.front: How do you approach Emergency short code?
cards.back: Put emergency rules above catch-alls, and give them a route that is always present. If it fails: A user dials 999 and the dial plan turns it into an extension.
A voice app that answers, plays a greeting, and routes by schedule, menu, directory, or operator. Why it matters: It is the front door. A broken menu is a broken company number.

cards.front: How do you approach Auto attendant?
cards.back: Create the attendant, attach a licensed resource account, then assign a number only if the PSTN must reach it. If it fails: The menu option points at a queue that has no agents and no overflow.

A voice app that holds callers and offers them to agents by attendant, serial, round robin, or longest idle routing. Why it matters: Presence can skip someone who is already busy, which changes who ‘should’ have rung.

cards.front: How do you approach Call queue?
cards.back: Set timeout and overflow before you publish the number. If it fails: The timeout is 3 seconds and callers always overflow.

A queue behavior where the caller stays in the conference while agents are tried, so the transfer is faster and the greeting is not replayed the same way. Why it matters: Turning it off changes the caller experience and the failure sound.

cards.front: How do you approach Conference mode?
cards.back: Test both modes with a real agent client before you argue about delay. If it fails: Callers hear silence while the queue hunts, and someone disables the queue.

Where the call goes when the queue is full or the timeout expires. It can be a person, another voice app, voicemail, or an external number. Why it matters: An external overflow needs funding on the resource account.
Name the overflow in the design, then test it by making every agent busy. If it fails: Overflow to a mobile fails and the queue itself is blamed.
An attendant feature that lets a caller reach a person by name or extension. Why it matters: It exposes the directory you did not mean to publish.

cards.front: How do you approach Directory search?
cards.back: Scope who can be found. Do not leave the default if the tenant has privileged accounts. If it fails: A caller reaches an executive because directory search was on.
A calendar the attendant uses to play the closed greeting. It is not the same object as business hours. Why it matters: A holiday that is only in someone’s memory is an open company on that day.

cards.front: How do you approach Holiday schedule?
cards.back: Load the next year’s holidays when you build the attendant. If it fails: The office is closed and the attendant still hunts the queue.
Teams picks a civic address from the network location it can see: trusted IP, site, and subnet in the usual design. Why it matters: A VPN address must not inherit the headquarters address.

cards.front: How do you approach Dynamic emergency calling?
cards.back: Build the topology, assign addresses, and test from a known subnet. If it fails: A laptop on the VPN reports the HQ floor.
The street address you validate for emergency calling. A dispatchable location is specific enough for responders. Why it matters: A campus with one address and five buildings is not specific.

cards.front: How do you approach Civic address?
cards.back: Validate the address and tie subnets to places inside it. If it fails: The PSAP gets a city and no building.

An address that means ‘this client is inside our network.’ It is how Teams decides the client is on a site you mapped. Why it matters: If the trusted IP is the VPN concentrator, every remote user looks internal.

cards.front: How do you approach Trusted IP?
cards.back: List the real internet egress addresses, not the VPN pool, unless you mean to. If it fails: Remote users inherit a building.
Controls notification and how the client looks up location. It is not the PSTN route. Why it matters: You can have a perfect policy and still send the call to the wrong SBC.

cards.front: How do you approach Emergency calling policy?
cards.back: Pair the policy with a routing policy and a tested number from the carrier. If it fails: Security is notified for a test call and the route still left the country.

You, the SBC, and the carrier deliver the emergency call. Microsoft does not become the emergency carrier because Teams is the client. Why it matters: PIDF-LO may be present. The carrier still has to accept the call.

cards.front: How do you approach Direct Routing emergency?
cards.back: Build an emergency voice route that prefers the local SBC. If it fails: 999 matches an international route via another country.

With Microsoft Calling Plans in supported countries, Microsoft’s emergency calling service is part of the plan. You still configure locations. Why it matters: Direct Routing habits do not apply unchanged.

cards.front: How do you approach Calling Plan emergency?
cards.back: Assign the Calling Plan and the emergency addresses for those users. If it fails: A Calling Plan user is sent to your SBC for 911 by a copied route.

Stops a user in a regulated site from placing a PSTN call through a gateway in another site. It is a toll-bypass control. Why it matters: Media bypass can fight it if media would egress in the wrong place.

cards.front: How do you approach Location-based routing?
cards.back: Enable it per site with the network topology and the gateways that belong there. If it fails: A traveler’s laptop in one country egresses through another country’s SBC.

A Direct Routing appliance that can keep local PSTN calling when the branch cannot reach Microsoft 365. Why it matters: It is not a full Teams cloud. Meetings and presence are not the survivable feature set.

cards.front: How do you approach Survivable Branch Appliance?
cards.back: Deploy a supported appliance, point the local clients at it, and test a WAN cut. If it fails: The office loses the WAN and nobody can call emergency services.

Media can flow between the Teams client and the SBC, skipping Microsoft’s media processors. Signaling still goes through Teams. Why it matters: People hear ‘bypass’ and think the SBC talks to Teams with no SIP proxy.

cards.front: How do you approach Media bypass?
cards.back: Enable it on the gateway only when the client can reach the SBC and LBR does not forbid the path. If it fails: Bypass is on for a VPN user and audio is worse than the processor path.
A Direct Routing pattern with internal and external SBC interfaces so a branch user stays on the local media path. Why it matters: It is more specific than a single bypass flag.

cards.front: How do you approach Local media optimization?
cards.back: Use the current media optimization article and the SBC vendor’s build. If it fails: Internal users hairpin out to the internet and back to the SBC on the same LAN.
Microsoft’s front end for certain compatible analog and SIP devices that are not Teams phones. Why it matters: It is not a substitute for a certified Direct Routing SBC.

cards.front: How do you approach SIP Gateway?
cards.back: Check the current supported device list before you buy handsets. If it fails: A generic analog adapter is plugged in and never registers.
A handset in Microsoft’s certified device program, signing in as a Teams user. Why it matters: An uncertified SIP phone will not behave like a Teams client.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams-certified phone?
cards.back: Buy from the current certified list and assign Teams Phone plus a number. If it fails: A bargain SIP phone is forced through SIP Gateway and the feature list is wrong.

The media encryption Direct Routing uses. Signaling is TLS. A successful INVITE with plaintext RTP is not the design. Why it matters: One-way audio is often a port problem, not a missing SRTP checkbox you invent.
Allow the UDP media range. Do not strip SRTP on the SBC. If it fails: The SBC offers RTP/AVP only and the call fails or is unsupported.
Direct Routing signaling expects modern TLS. TLS 1.0 is not a compatible offer. Why it matters: Old SBC firmware is a certificate problem and a protocol problem at once.
Upgrade firmware and offer TLS 1.2 or newer toward the proxies. If it fails: The handshake dies before OPTIONS.

The name on the SBC certificate must match the FQDN you paired. Wildcards are allowed when they follow RFC 2818. Why it matters: A certificate that is valid for the website and not for sbc1.contoso.com still fails.

cards.front: How do you approach Certificate SAN?
cards.back: Issue the certificate for the paired name. Include the chain. If it fails: TLS fails with a name mismatch and someone restarts the SBC.

The SBC certificate must come from a CA in Microsoft’s trusted root program. A private lab CA is not enough for production pairing. Why it matters: Lab trunks that use a private CA teach the wrong lesson.

cards.front: How do you approach Microsoft trusted root?
cards.back: Use a public CA for the production FQDN. If it fails: The trunk works in the lab and fails the morning you point it at sip.pstnhub.
The certificate should include the server authentication extended key usage. Why it matters: A client-auth-only certificate is the wrong object.

cards.front: How do you approach Server Authentication EKU?
cards.back: Request the certificate from the SBC’s CSR so the name and the EKU are right. If it fails: The chain is trusted and the EKU is still wrong.
The per-user, per-call quality view in the Teams admin center. Use it when one person had one bad call. Why it matters: It will not explain a building. That is CQD.

cards.front: How do you approach Call Analytics?
cards.back: Open the user’s call and read jitter, loss, and RTT on each stream. If it fails: A site problem is hunted one user at a time.
The aggregate quality report. Use it for subnets, buildings, and trends. Why it matters: A single angry caller is the wrong entry point.

cards.front: How do you approach Call Quality Dashboard?
cards.back: Confirm the subnet-to-building map before you trust a building chart. If it fails: HQ looks terrible because the VPN pool was labeled HQ.

Teach yourself to look at jitter, packet loss, and round-trip time separately. A mark of DSCP 0 plus high jitter is a different fault from 12% loss with EF still set. Why it matters: One ‘poor’ label hides the cause.

cards.front: How do you approach Poor stream clues?
cards.back: Capture at the egress and compare with CQD. If it fails: The ticket says ‘Teams is down’ and loss is 0.2% with a 600 ms RTT.
A time-ordered picture of requests and responses between client, proxy, SBC, and carrier, joined by Call-ID. Why it matters: Without the Call-ID you are looking at two different calls.

cards.front: How do you approach SIP ladder?
cards.back: Capture on the SBC, filter the Call-ID, and read the first non-success code. If it fails: Two captures are compared and they are different calls.
Change one thing, then collect the same evidence again. A reboot plus a dial-plan edit plus a firewall change teaches nothing. Why it matters: Voice bridges punish bundled changes.

cards.front: How do you approach One hypothesis?
cards.back: Write the hypothesis, the change, and the capture you expect. If it fails: Three vendors change three boxes and the call starts working for an unknown reason.

Microsoft’s contact-center product. It can stand alone or sit with Customer Service. Voice uses Azure Communication Services under the covers. Why it matters: It is not an auto attendant with extra steps.

cards.front: How do you approach Dynamics 365 Contact Center?
cards.back: Deploy the environment, the channels, and unified routing before you demo Copilot. If it fails: A pilot turns on Copilot and never defines a queue.

The representative experience in Dynamics. Contact Center can embed there or run as its own product surface. Why it matters: Buying Customer Service does not automatically give you the contact-center voice channel.

cards.front: How do you approach Customer Service workspace?
cards.back: Confirm embedded versus standalone in the current implementation guide. If it fails: Agents look for the queue in the wrong app.
The intake pipe in unified routing. It classifies work and sends it to a queue. Why it matters: A channel with no workstream is a number that rings nowhere useful.
Create the workstream, then the rules, then the queues. If it fails: Chat and voice land in the same queue with no skill rules.
Rules that set skills, intent, or priority on a work item before assignment. Why it matters: Without classification, capacity and skills have nothing to read.

cards.front: How do you approach Work classification?
cards.back: Test with two items that should land in different queues. If it fails: French callers reach the English queue.
How many items of each type a representative can hold. A voice call usually consumes more than a chat message. Why it matters: Agents look idle in one channel and overloaded in another.

cards.front: How do you approach Capacity profile?
cards.back: Set capacity, then watch a test item get stuck when the number is zero. If it fails: The queue has agents and every item overflows.
The human on the contact-center side. AB-250 calls the console the representative experience. Why it matters: Do not confuse this person with a Teams resource account.
Give them a security role, a capacity profile, and a queue membership. If it fails: The user can open the app and is not a member of any queue.
Assistive summaries, suggested replies, and knowledge inside the representative experience. It is not the PSTN route. Why it matters: A summary of the wrong case is worse than no summary.

cards.front: How do you approach Copilot in the contact center?
cards.back: Connect knowledge sources and test on a known case. If it fails: Copilot answers from a stale article and the agent sends it.

The published AB-250 study guide weights channel implementation at about 30–35 percent, the largest slice. Why it matters: People over-study Copilot and under-study voice, chat, and the other channels.

cards.front: How do you approach AB-250 channels weight?
cards.back: Spend the study time on channel setup and routing. If it fails: An exam candidate can describe Copilot and cannot trace a voice channel.

A certified contact center attaches to Teams through certified SBCs and Direct Routing. Why it matters: Microsoft’s note: the contact-center agent does not need a phone-system license for that solution; a Teams user who receives a transfer does.

cards.front: How do you approach Connect model?
cards.back: Confirm the vendor’s current certification, then design the SBC and the transfer target’s license. If it fails: Transfers to experts fail because the expert has no Teams Phone number.

The contact center uses the Teams client, Graph, and Cloud Communications APIs. Teams Phone is the calling system and the agent works in Teams. Why it matters: This is not ‘we also installed their desktop.’

cards.front: How do you approach Extend model?
cards.back: Read the Extend section of the contact-center article before you license agents. If it fails: The design buys a Connect SBC for an Extend product.

The model Microsoft Learn names, as of 14 October 2026, for a native experience. Partner material describes it as ACS-based applications on Teams calling infrastructure. Older decks say Power. Ask which current model a vendor holds. Why it matters: Licensing and media follow the model, not the sales adjective.

cards.front: How do you approach Unify model?
cards.back: Get the vendor’s certification letter and match it to Connect, Extend, or Unify. If it fails: A proposal says Power and nobody can find the media path.
A way for a contact center, including Dynamics 365 Contact Center, to use a customer’s existing Teams Phone for the agent’s telephony. Why it matters: It is not a second carrier hidden in the app.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams Phone extensibility?
cards.back: Use a solution that has finished the certification if you want the supported experience. The API existing is not the same as a finished certification. If it fails: Two phone systems ring the same person.

Cisco Unified Border Element can be the certified SBC between Teams and CUCM or a carrier. The IOS-XE release you run has its own guide. Why it matters: This campus does not paste a production dial-peer.

cards.front: How do you approach CUBE as a bridge?
cards.back: TLS to the three proxies, a certificate whose name matches the paired FQDN, and dial-peers toward CUCM. If it fails: Early offer and codec preferences are left at a lab default and calls 488.
During coexistence, either Teams or CUCM should transform numbers, not both. Why it matters: Double +44 is a classic dual-running fault.

cards.front: How do you approach One normalization owner?
cards.back: Write the owner on the design and test a call in each direction. If it fails: CUCM adds a prefix and the Teams dial plan adds it again.

A call from a user who stayed on CUCM to a user who moved to Teams hairpins through the SBC. It is normal during dual-running and expensive as a steady state. Why it matters: Media and licenses both feel it.
Move groups that call each other in the same wave. If it fails: The carrier bill rises and nobody left the building.
A SIP trunk through a local gateway or CUBE can carry calls between Webex Calling users and Teams users during a split estate. Why it matters: Chat interoperability is a different project from voice.

cards.front: How do you approach Webex calling bridge?
cards.back: Treat it as coexistence with one numbering plan, not as a merger. If it fails: Two dial plans both own the same range.

Contact-center agents can stay on CVP and Finesse while knowledge workers move to Teams. The SBC sends contact-center numbers one way and user numbers another. Why it matters: Putting an agent on a Teams client does not keep the CVP script in control.

cards.front: How do you approach UCCE coexistence?
cards.back: Split the dial plan by number range and test a transfer to an expert on Teams. If it fails: Agents move first and the IVR script can no longer see them.
Genesys sells contact-center integrations with Teams. The certification model, Connect, Extend, or Unify, decides the media path and the licenses. Why it matters: Do not assume last year’s diagram.

cards.front: How do you approach Genesys and Teams?
cards.back: Ask for the current Microsoft certification and design to that model. If it fails: The statement of work says certified and does not name the model.

A customer pattern uses an SBC between Teams Direct Routing and Amazon Connect or a SIP voice connector. It is a bridge you design, not a Microsoft Calling Plan feature. Why it matters: Confirm the current vendor docs before you promise agent whisper or recording.

cards.front: How do you approach Amazon Connect and Teams?
cards.back: Draw the SIP path and the identifier you will store. If it fails: Both platforms record and neither capture has the Call-ID.

The ACS server-side calling API. Your app answers, plays, recognizes DTMF or speech, and transfers. You receive events. You do not drive a desktop click. Why it matters: It is the IVR runtime, not the Teams client.

cards.front: How do you approach Call Automation?
cards.back: Subscribe to the events and time out the recognize step. If it fails: The app never answers, so the caller hears ringing until the platform gives up.
The ACS client SDK for a human in a browser or a mobile app. Different from Call Automation, which is the server. Why it matters: Teams interop has its own requirements on top of either one.

cards.front: How do you approach Calling SDK?
cards.back: Pick the SDK if a person is on the page. Pick automation if a bot answers. If it fails: A web page uses the calling SDK and nobody handles the server events.
The Call Automation action that collects DTMF or speech. It needs a timeout and a path for ‘none of the above.’ Why it matters: A recognize step without an escape traps the caller.

cards.front: How do you approach Recognize step?
cards.back: Map 0 to a human queue and test it. If it fails: The bot repeats the prompt until the caller hangs up.

Microsoft’s speech-to-text and text-to-speech service. Copilot Studio and custom IVRs can use it. It is not emergency calling. Why it matters: A custom neural voice has its own approval rules. Do not assume you can clone a person.

cards.front: How do you approach Azure AI Speech?
cards.back: Choose a voice you are allowed to use and log the recognition result. If it fails: The prompt language does not match the caller and every intent is unknown.

A bot built in Copilot Studio that can front a voice channel, including Dynamics contact-center voice, using topics or generative orchestration. Why it matters: Generative answers still need an escape to a human and a knowledge source you trust.

cards.front: How do you approach Copilot Studio voice agent?
cards.back: Publish the agent, attach it to the channel, and test the escape digit. If it fails: The agent is the only target of the public number, including emergencies.
The Azure portal family for models, agents, and evaluations. The earlier name was Azure AI Studio. It does not route PSTN. Why it matters: A model demo is not a contact-center design.

cards.front: How do you approach Azure AI Foundry?
cards.back: Evaluate a prompt against a test set before you put it on a phone number. If it fails: A model change ships to the IVR with no eval.
ACS can be set up to call Teams users and to join Teams meetings when the interop prerequisites are met. Why it matters: A raw ACS number does not automatically become a Teams user.

cards.front: How do you approach Teams interop with ACS?
cards.back: Follow the current interop article for the resource you created. If it fails: The bot can call the PSTN and cannot transfer to a Teams expert.

MS-700 is still live, with a skills update on Oct 27 2026; it is NOT retired and has no replacement. It is the exam for Microsoft 365 Certified: Teams Administrator Associate. Why it matters: Rumors that it was replaced by an MS-220 collaboration exam are not what Learn says.
Study the current guide, including network and call-quality objectives. There is no replacement exam. If it fails: A candidate skips networking because they think the exam is only meetings.

MB-280 retired Jul 31 2026, with AB-210 as its successor; AB-210 is in beta. It covered Sales and Customer Insights, not the contact-center product. Why it matters: People still put it on a contact-center study plan.

cards.front: How do you approach MB-280 retired?
cards.back: Do not book MB-280. AB-210 is its successor and is in beta. AB-250 is the contact-center exam. If it fails: A job post requires MB-280 after the retirement date.
Dynamics 365 Sales AI Consultant Associate. AB-210 is the successor to MB-280 and is in beta. It is not a replacement for MS-700. Why it matters: It is the wrong exam for a contact-center engineer.
Use AB-250 when the job is Dynamics 365 Contact Center. Use AB-210 only for a sales role, and remember it is in beta. If it fails: Study time goes to sales Copilot for a queue-routing role.

Transforming Contact Center Experiences with AI in Dynamics 365. It earns Dynamics 365 Contact Center AI Engineer Associate. Pass mark is 700. The public page allows 120 minutes. Why it matters: The beta discount ran through 18 June 2026. Confirm the seat you can book now.
Study deploy, channels, agents, work distribution, the representative experience, and analytics. If it fails: A candidate revises MB-280 practice tests for this exam.
Azure Fundamentals. It was not on the retirement list reviewed on 14 October 2026. Why it matters: Useful context for ACS and Speech. It will not teach you a dial plan.
Take it if you need Azure vocabulary, not instead of MS-700. If it fails: A voice design is approved because someone passed AZ-900.
Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals. The English certification is scheduled to update on 21 October 2026. Why it matters: It frames Entra ID and compliance. It does not configure an SBC.
Read the current study guide after the 21 October update if you sit it later. If it fails: Conditional Access is treated as out of scope for a voice project.
Microsoft 365 Fundamentals retired on 31 March 2026. Why it matters: Do not recommend it as the starting exam.

cards.front: How do you approach MS-900 retired?
cards.back: Use role exams and the product docs. If it fails: A learning path still tells a new hire to book MS-900.
Azure AI Fundamentals retired on 30 June 2026. Why it matters: Speech and Copilot Studio are learned from their own docs now.

cards.front: How do you approach AI-900 retired?
cards.back: Do not use a retired fundamentals exam as the AI plan. If it fails: The study plan lists AI-900 beside AB-250.
Microsoft role-based exams, including MS-700 and AB-250, require 700 out of 1000. Why it matters: A practice percentage is not the same scale unless the practice says so.

cards.front: How do you approach Passing score 700?
cards.back: Use the official practice assessment when one exists. If it fails: Someone stops studying at a 70 percent practice score on a different scale.

A user starts a recording of a call, meeting, or event. Policy can allow it. The user can stop it. Storage follows meeting rules. Why it matters: It is not a compliance program. Guests cannot start it.

cards.front: How do you approach Convenience recording?
cards.back: Set the meeting, calling, and events policies on purpose. If it fails: A regulated desk is told to ‘just hit record.’

A third-party recorder is invited by policy into new calls, meetings, and events. The user does not start it and participant consent is not the control. Notification is enforced. Why it matters: The comparison table says audio-only is not the compliance mode. Media listed is voice, video, and screen share.

cards.front: How do you approach Compliance recording?
cards.back: Create the application instance, enable the policy, grant it, and test a new call. If it fails: The policy is granted and nothing records because the bot instance was never created.

The bot instance of a certified recorder. The policy references it. Without it, granting the policy does not record. Why it matters: Work with the recorder vendor for the application ID. Do not invent one.

cards.front: How do you approach Compliance recording application?
cards.back: New-CsTeamsComplianceRecordingApplication attaches it to the policy. If it fails: Recording works in the vendor’s cloud and never joins the Teams call.
When you grant a compliance recording policy, calls and meetings already up are not swept in. Test with a new call. Why it matters: A pilot that reuses an open meeting proves nothing.

cards.front: How do you approach Existing calls are unaffected?
cards.back: Place a fresh call after the grant and confirm the bot joined. If it fails: The pilot says recording failed because they watched an old meeting.

Listening to and scoring recorded interactions. Often the same vendor as compliance recording, sometimes a separate one. Why it matters: QM needs the recording first. A score without audio is a rumor.

cards.front: How do you approach Quality management?
cards.back: Define the form, the sample, and who may listen. If it fails: Supervisors export recordings to a laptop share.
Scheduling and adherence for a queue. It eats interval stats, handle time, and shrinkage. It is not a feature of a Teams user policy. Why it matters: Teams Call Analytics will not staff next Tuesday.

cards.front: How do you approach Workforce management?
cards.back: Feed offered, answered, abandoned, and handle time from the queue or the CCaaS. If it fails: WFM says you were overstaffed while the queue overflowed, because overflow removed the calls from the count.

The fraction of paid time that is not available for contacts: leave, training, meetings, breaks. Why it matters: Erlang C tells you how many people must be on the phone. Shrinkage tells you how many to roster.
Publish the assumption. A 30 percent guess should be labeled as a guess. If it fails: The schedule staffs the Erlang number and half the team is in training.
Handle time divided by handle time plus available time. High occupancy feels efficient and burns people out. Why it matters: WFM and quality fight here.
Watch it beside service level, not instead of service level. If it fails: A site celebrates 95 percent occupancy and abandonment climbs.
The fraction of contacts answered inside a target, for example 80 percent in 20 seconds. Erlang C is one teaching model of it. Why it matters: Averages hide the tail.

cards.front: How do you approach Service level?
cards.back: Write the target, the interval, and the abandonment rule. If it fails: Two vendors compute abandoned calls differently and both claim the target.

Power BI can sit on top of Call Quality Dashboard data. It does not replace Call Analytics for one call, and it inherits a bad subnet map. Why it matters: A pretty report of the wrong building is still wrong.

cards.front: How do you approach Power BI and CQD?
cards.back: Fix the building and subnet dimensions before you publish a dashboard. If it fails: Leadership sees a red HQ that is actually the VPN pool.

The CRM opens the contact that matches the caller. Teams does not do this by itself for an ordinary PSTN call. Why it matters: The contact center or a middleware has to pass an E.164 number or a case id.

cards.front: How do you approach Screen pop?
cards.back: Normalize before the lookup. Store the Call-ID on the timeline. If it fails: The pop shows the wrong person because the trunk prefix was still on the number.

The international form of a number, starting with + and a country code. Routes and CRM lookups should use it after normalization. Why it matters: Raw digits mean different things in different countries.
Normalize first, then route, then look up. If it fails: The CRM stores 0207… and the SBC stores +44207… and they never join.

The SIP header that identifies one dialog. It is the join key between an SBC capture, a carrier ticket, and a CRM note. Why it matters: A timestamp is not an identifier. Two calls start in the same second.
Write the Call-ID into the system you will have open during an incident. If it fails: Support has a CRM case and an SBC log and cannot prove they are the same call.
A named place where another system is allowed to attach: a policy, a queue overflow, a subnet list, an event, an identifier. Why it matters: A seam you do not name becomes a rewrite.

cards.front: How do you approach Integration seam?
cards.back: Document the seam in the same change as the feature. If it fails: Recording is added a year later and the number plan has to change.
A digit or intent that always reaches a person. Voice agents need one. Emergency numbers need a real route, not a bot. Why it matters: A bot that cannot fail open will trap callers.

cards.front: How do you approach Human escape?
cards.back: Test the escape on every prompt change. If it fails: The prompt says ‘say agent’ and the recognize step has no such intent.

The date the SBC certificate stops being valid. It is an integration hook because every carrier and every proxy will notice it on the same morning. Why it matters: Calendar it like a license, not like a surprise.

cards.front: How do you approach Certificate expiry seam?
cards.back: Monitor the date and renew before the TLS handshake fails. If it fails: OPTIONS fail on a Saturday and the dial plan is blamed.
The same subnet definitions should feed emergency location, location-based routing, and the CQD building report. Why it matters: Three spreadsheets drift.

cards.front: How do you approach Subnet as a shared list?
cards.back: Give one team the edit right and publish the list. If it fails: E911 says London, CQD says VPN, LBR says Manchester.

A 15-minute or 30-minute bucket of offered, answered, and abandoned contacts. WFM and Erlang C both assume you know the bucket. Why it matters: Mixing daily totals into a 30-minute formula is a unit error.

cards.front: How do you approach Queue interval?
cards.back: Export the same interval the schedule uses. If it fails: The forecast is ten times too high because the interval was a day.
A caller who hangs up before an agent answers. Whether short abandons count is a business rule. Why it matters: Two reports with different abandon rules cannot be compared.
Write the rule down and use it in WFM and in the service-level report. If it fails: Service level is met only because abandons under five seconds were deleted.

Talk time plus after-call work, unless your definition says otherwise. Erlang traffic is calls times handle time divided by the interval. Why it matters: A handle time that forgets after-call work understaffs the queue.

cards.front: How do you approach Average handle time?
cards.back: Measure it from the contact center, not from a stopwatch on one call. If it fails: The Erlang sheet uses talk time only and the agents never finish wrap-up.

A location object that can be carried in a SIP INVITE for an emergency call so the far end sees where the caller is. Why it matters: It does not replace a carrier who knows how to route emergency calls in that country.
Confirm the SBC passes it and the carrier reads it. If it fails: The location is stripped at the SBC and the PSAP gets the trunk’s address only.
An emergency calling policy can notify people on site when an emergency call is placed. Why it matters: Security who are not notified will meet the responders in the wrong lobby.

cards.front: How do you approach On-site notification?
cards.back: Test the notification with the carrier’s test process, not with a real emergency call. If it fails: The test notifies nobody because the policy was never assigned.

Office 365 GCC High uses sip.pstnhub.gov.teams.microsoft.us. Do not copy the commercial three-proxy list into a government tenant. Why it matters: The commercial names will not be the signaling peers.

cards.front: How do you approach GCC High SIP?
cards.back: Read the plan page for the cloud you are actually in. If it fails: A commercial runbook is pasted into GCC High.
Office 365 DoD uses sip.pstnhub.dod.teams.microsoft.us. Why it matters: Same failure as using commercial names in the wrong cloud.

cards.front: How do you approach DoD SIP?
cards.back: Use the DoD name from the current plan page. If it fails: The SBC peers with sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com from a DoD tenant.

The plan page also lists sip.ipv6.pstnhub.microsoft.com and the sip2 and sip3 IPv6 names, resolving into 2603:1063:400::/40. Why it matters: An IPv6-only SBC that was given the IPv4 names never peers.

cards.front: How do you approach IPv6 SIP proxies?
cards.back: Match the address family you actually route. If it fails: Firewall objects exist only for IPv4.
Teams Direct Routing presents media in the INVITE. An SBC or CUBE that waits for a delayed offer will negotiate badly. Why it matters: 488 and one-way audio show up when the offer model is wrong.

cards.front: How do you approach Early offer?
cards.back: Set the vendor profile for early offer toward Teams. If it fails: CUCM sends delayed offer all the way to Teams.

A certified SBC family. Mediant devices and their management tools are common in Direct Routing designs. The Microsoft certified list is the support boundary, the vendor guide is the config. Why it matters: Naming the brand is not a design.
Follow AudioCodes’ current Teams document for the firmware you run. If it fails: A forum config from 2019 is pasted onto new firmware.
Ribbon’s certified session border controllers are a Direct Routing option. Core and software editions differ. Why it matters: The support path is Ribbon first, then Microsoft if the vendor escalates.

cards.front: How do you approach Ribbon SBC?
cards.back: Use Ribbon’s current Teams guide and a public certificate. If it fails: OPTIONS are answered on the wrong interface.

Oracle Communications Session Border Controller can be certified for Direct Routing on specific releases. Check the Microsoft list for the release, not the logo. Why it matters: An unlisted release is an unsupported trunk.

cards.front: How do you approach Oracle SBC?
cards.back: Match the certified software version and the certificate name. If it fails: The beautiful config is one release below the certified list.

Cisco Unified Border Element on IOS-XE, when the release is certified, is a normal Direct Routing SBC and the usual bridge to CUCM. Why it matters: CUBE is still an SBC. It does not make Teams ‘speak SCCP.’

cards.front: How do you approach Cisco CUBE?
cards.back: Use Cisco’s current CUBE for Teams guide. Trust the signaling ranges. Present the paired name. If it fails: A voice engineer applies a SIP trunk to CUCM and never peers with the pstnhub names.

Microsoft’s Direct Routing support boundary: you call the SBC vendor, they escalate to Microsoft if they must. Non-certified SBCs can be refused. Why it matters: Opening a Microsoft case with a homemade SBC wastes the outage.

cards.front: How do you approach Vendor-first support?
cards.back: Keep the certified-list screenshot with the firmware version. If it fails: A ticket is opened with no SBC logs and no firmware.
Fax, door phones, and elevators usually stay on an SBC or SIP Gateway, not on a Teams client. Why it matters: A Calling Plan user license does not give you an elevator phone.

cards.front: How do you approach Analog via Direct Routing?
cards.back: Put analog on the SBC design and test the emergency path from that device. If it fails: The elevator is moved to Teams as a user and cannot dial during a WAN cut.

A queue can skip agents whose Teams presence says they are busy or in a meeting. Why it matters: An agent who never sets presence will take every serial call or none, depending on the rest of the design.

cards.front: How do you approach Presence-based routing?
cards.back: Decide the presence rule and test with one agent in a meeting. If it fails: Agents set themselves to Do Not Disturb to leave the queue, and nobody notices for a week.

Agents can be allowed to leave a queue. If you forbid it, staffing math must include breaks or they will dodge in other ways. Why it matters: WFM adherence and the queue opt-out flag are the same argument.

cards.front: How do you approach Opt out of a queue?
cards.back: Pick one policy and tell the supervisors. If it fails: The schedule says five agents and three have opted out.

A queue feature that calls the customer back. The prerequisite article treats callback as a case that needs funding on the resource account. Why it matters: Callback is an outbound PSTN call, not a setting with no carrier.
Fund pay-as-you-go or credits, then test one callback. If it fails: The option is on and every callback fails.

Microsoft Graph APIs used by Extend and by recording and presence integrations. They are not a SIP trunk. Why it matters: A design that says ‘we will use Graph instead of an SBC’ still needs a PSTN path.

cards.front: How do you approach Graph communications?
cards.back: Use Graph for the app, and Calling Plans, Operator Connect, or Direct Routing for the telephone network. If it fails: Presence is synced and audio is not connected.

The recorder joins as an application because the user’s policy names it. If the bot fails to join, you have a policy, an ID, or a media problem, in that order. Why it matters: Do not start with the carrier.

cards.front: How do you approach Policy recording bot join?
cards.back: Check Enabled, the application instance, and the grant, then the vendor’s join log. If it fails: The carrier is asked for a recording they never made.

Compliance recordings are retained by the partner’s system, not by Teams meeting storage. Convenience recordings follow meeting storage. Why it matters: Legal hold on a mailbox does not automatically hold the partner’s audio.

cards.front: How do you approach Retention of recordings?
cards.back: Write the retention in the partner contract and test a restore. If it fails: A regulator asks for a call and the partner’s bucket expired.
The QM scorecard. It should cite behaviors you can hear, not vibes. Why it matters: A form that scores ‘professionalism’ without a definition will not survive an argument.

cards.front: How do you approach Evaluation form?
cards.back: Publish the form before you score people. If it fails: Agents are coached on a form they have never seen.

Often a QM vendor feature on the agent desktop. Teams compliance recording’s documented media list is voice, video, and screen share inside the Teams session, which is not the same as a silent desktop recorder. Why it matters: Do not claim Teams records the CRM screen unless the product you bought does.

cards.front: How do you approach Screen recording?
cards.back: If you need the desktop, buy and disclose that recorder. If it fails: A privacy review finds a desktop recorder nobody mentioned.
The table that says which subnet is which building in CQD. It is only as good as the subnets you typed. Why it matters: A wrong building makes a dashboard accuse the wrong LAN.

cards.front: How do you approach Building map?
cards.back: Reconcile it with the emergency subnet list. If it fails: Facilities rebuilds a floor and both maps stay old.

CQD is an admin report, not a personal call history. The people who can open it are the roles you grant, not every user. Why it matters: A manager with no role will ask for a screenshot instead of access.

cards.front: How do you approach Admin roles for CQD?
cards.back: Grant the smallest role that can see the report. If it fails: CQD credentials are shared.
Time the agent spends in the CRM after the caller hangs up. Include it in handle time if your WFM definition says so. Why it matters: Leaving it out makes Erlang C look generous.

cards.front: How do you approach After-call work?
cards.back: Define it and measure it from the contact-center state, not from memory. If it fails: Agents are ‘available’ in Teams while still writing the case.
Assignment that prefers a representative who has the skill the classification step wrote on the work item. Why it matters: Skills that exist on a slide and not on the user do nothing.

cards.front: How do you approach Skill-based routing?
cards.back: Attach skills to people and to the classification rules, then test a miss. If it fails: Every item requires a skill nobody has, so the queue never assigns.
Classification that uses an intent, often from a bot or a model, to pick a queue. Why it matters: An intent of ‘unknown’ needs a default queue.

cards.front: How do you approach Intent-based routing?
cards.back: Map unknown to a human, not to a retry loop. If it fails: The model returns unknown and the caller is played the same prompt.
Contact-center campaigns that place calls outward. They need a number, a consent story, and a capacity plan. Why it matters: They are not a Teams user’s personal redial.

cards.front: How do you approach Proactive outbound?
cards.back: Follow the current channel article for outbound, and fund the numbers. If it fails: A campaign uses a user’s caller ID and the CRM trust collapses.

A channel feature that can translate a conversation. It is not a substitute for a language queue when the policy says a human must speak the language. Why it matters: Translation errors in a regulated script are your errors.

cards.front: How do you approach Real-time translation?
cards.back: Decide where translation is allowed and where a skilled human is required. If it fails: A billing dispute is translated badly and the case notes disagree.
The documents a Copilot or a generative agent is allowed to quote. If the source is wrong, the answer is wrong with confidence. Why it matters: Ground the agent or do not put it on the phone.

cards.front: How do you approach Knowledge source?
cards.back: Limit the sources and test questions whose answers you already know. If it fails: The agent quotes a retired price list.
The Copilot Studio mode that chooses topics and tools from the conversation, as opposed to a rigid topic tree. Why it matters: It needs tighter safety because the path is not a single menu.

cards.front: How do you approach Generative orchestration?
cards.back: Keep the human escape outside the model’s mood. If it fails: The agent talks a caller out of the escape phrase.
The menu-like Copilot Studio design. Predictable and easier to test. Weaker on paraphrase. Why it matters: Use it when the call must follow a script.

cards.front: How do you approach Classic topics?
cards.back: Write the topics, the entities, and the fallback. If it fails: Fallback is empty and the caller hears silence.
One way ACS delivers call events to your app. If the subscription is wrong, your IVR never sees RecognizeCompleted. Why it matters: The call can be up and your code asleep.

cards.front: How do you approach Event Grid?
cards.back: Log the event type and the call id. If it fails: The app polls a database and the events expired.
Digits in the audio path or as telephone-events. IVRs fail when the SBC strips them. Why it matters: A human can talk and the bot never hears 1.

cards.front: How do you approach DTMF relay?
cards.back: Test digits through every SBC, not only Teams-to-Teams. If it fails: The queue escape works in the lab and fails through the carrier.

Silence suppression changes the average bitrate. Do not size a link only from a G.711 average that assumed comfort noise you did not enable. Why it matters: The peak is still the number that fills the queue.

cards.front: How do you approach Comfort noise and SID?
cards.back: Size for the codec you offer, per direction, at the packetization you set. If it fails: The link was sized for silence and the all-hands call filled it.
The usual voice packet interval in these bandwidth figures. A 10 ms interval doubles the header tax. Why it matters: Changing ptime on the SBC changes the bandwidth you planned.

cards.front: How do you approach Packetization 20 ms?
cards.back: Lock ptime in the design. If it fails: One SBC uses 10 ms and the policer drops packets.

The client waits a little so late packets can still be played. Too small and you hear gaps. Too large and you talk over each other. Why it matters: CQD jitter and the buffer are related and not the same number.

cards.front: How do you approach Jitter buffer?
cards.back: Fix the network before you hunt a hidden buffer setting. If it fails: A WAN with 40 ms jitter is ‘fixed’ by a slide that says buffer.
How long a packet takes to go and come back. Long RTT with low loss means distance or hairpin, not a dirty cable. Why it matters: People add bandwidth and the delay stays.

cards.front: How do you approach Round-trip time?
cards.back: Look at the path. Bypass or local egress may beat a fatter pipe. If it fails: A branch backhauls media across a continent.
A router or VPN that sets the mark back to 0. The client did its job and the path undid it. Why it matters: Verify at the egress, not only on the PC.

cards.front: How do you approach DSCP rewrite?
cards.back: Capture outside the VPN. If it fails: The laptop shows EF and the WAN sees 0.

People who join meetings in a browser do not use the fixed 50000-range client ports. An ACL that only matches those ports misses them. Why it matters: QoS designs that ignore browsers miss a real population.

cards.front: How do you approach Browser join ports?
cards.back: Say so in the design if many people join from browsers. If it fails: Guests sound worse and the ACL is declared complete.
Mac, iOS, and Android use hard-coded audio EF and a hard-coded video and sharing mark. They are not the Windows policy object. Why it matters: A Windows-only QoS rollout looks done and is not.

cards.front: How do you approach Mac and mobile DSCP?
cards.back: Still enable QoS in the admin center, and mark at the network for devices that will not cooperate. If it fails: Mobile executives are the poor-quality population.

The current Teams client process name used when you bind a Windows QoS policy. An old policy aimed at the classic client marks nothing. Why it matters: Policy that matches the wrong executable is a silent miss.
Update the policy object and verify with a capture. If it fails: QoS policy still names the previous client.
The hour you actually size. Average day divided by eight is not a busy hour. Why it matters: Erlang inputs are busy-interval numbers.

cards.front: How do you approach Busy hour?
cards.back: Take the busy interval from the contact center, not from a yearly average. If it fails: The link is fine at 11:00 and dead at 09:15.
Both PBX and Teams carry live numbers during a move. Rollback needs the old route left intact. Why it matters: A cut with no rollback is a career event.

cards.front: How do you approach Dual running?
cards.back: Move a range, keep the old path, and write the backout. If it fails: The old trunk is deleted on Friday.

Moving a public number from one carrier to another. It has a date and a letter of authority. It is not a PowerShell metaphor. Why it matters: Direct Routing can use numbers the carrier already holds, so a port might be unnecessary.

cards.front: How do you approach Number porting?
cards.back: Confirm who owns the number before you promise a weekend cut. If it fails: Two carriers route the same number on Monday.
What outbound calls present. Resource-account outbound and user outbound are different policies. Why it matters: A queue that presents a user’s mobile number breaks trust.

cards.front: How do you approach Caller ID policy?
cards.back: Set the calling identity on the voice app on purpose. If it fails: Customers return a call and reach an employee’s personal desk.

The audio a queue plays while a caller waits. Licensing and the file both matter, and silence is a choice you should make on purpose. Why it matters: Callers who hear nothing hang up, and abandon looks like a staffing crisis.

cards.front: How do you approach Music on hold?
cards.back: Upload a file you have rights to, and test the timeout. If it fails: A licensed song is uploaded.

A respectable overflow target when nobody is left to answer. It depends on Cloud Voicemail and a mailbox for the account that owns it. Why it matters: Overflow to voicemail without a mailbox is a dead end.

cards.front: How do you approach Voicemail overflow?
cards.back: Test the overflow, then check that the message arrived. If it fails: Callers are offered voicemail and the message is never deposited.
The public number on the first voice app. Everything else can be an internal target. Why it matters: People buy a number per menu option and then cannot afford to change the menu.

cards.front: How do you approach Pilot number?
cards.back: One number, many targets, overflow included. If it fails: Each menu option is a ported number and the carrier lead time runs the project.
Compliance recording and many Teams policies can be assigned to a group. A user in the wrong group is recorded, or not, as a consequence. Why it matters: Group sprawl is a voice defect.

cards.front: How do you approach Security group policy assign?
cards.back: Use a group you can explain, and read the effective policy. If it fails: A contractor group inherits recording and a privacy review fails.
The policy the user actually has after direct assignment and group assignment are resolved. The one you edited may not be it. Why it matters: Get-CsOnlineUser beats the portal memory.

cards.front: How do you approach Effective policy?
cards.back: Read the effective value before and after the change. If it fails: You update a policy that is not assigned.
A tenant that is not production. Pair a lab SBC there. Do not discover certificate behavior on the company trunk. Why it matters: Production is where rollback costs money.

cards.front: How do you approach Lab tenant?
cards.back: Keep lab domains and lab certificates obvious. If it fails: A lab FQDN is the production FQDN.
Cmdlet parameters move between MicrosoftTeams module versions. Read help in the version you are about to run. Why it matters: A blog’s parameter list is not a contract.

cards.front: How do you approach Get-Help before Set?
cards.back: Get-Help cmdlet -Parameter * in the lab. If it fails: A script from last year removes a number.
Use the telephony or communications role that can do the task. Global Administrator is not a voice habit. Why it matters: A shared global account makes every later audit useless.

cards.front: How do you approach Least privilege?
cards.back: Named admin accounts, voice roles, and Conditional Access for admins. If it fails: The SBC password and the global admin password are the same sticky note.

A number assigned to a resource account or conferencing, as opposed to a user’s personal number. The inventory and the license follow the connectivity option. Why it matters: A user number on a queue is how you lose the queue when the human leaves.

cards.front: How do you approach Service number?
cards.back: Take service numbers from the carrier or Calling Plan inventory you actually have. If it fails: The receptionist leaves and the main number leaves with them.

What Teams does with a number you own that is not assigned. Routing it to an attendant is a product choice you should make. Why it matters: Silence on a published-but-unassigned number looks like an outage.

cards.front: How do you approach Unassigned number treatment?
cards.back: Point unknown numbers at an attendant or a message. If it fails: A ported block has fifty silent numbers.

This campus treats repeated missed OPTIONS as a reason to pull a trunk. It does not publish Microsoft’s internal counter as if it were a documented integer. Why it matters: A lab timer is not a contractual timer.

cards.front: How do you approach SIP options timer teaching model?
cards.back: Watch the admin-center SBC status and the SBC’s own OPTIONS log together. If it fails: Someone sets a script to fail over after one missed packet and flaps the trunk.
Pull the primary proxy or the primary SBC in a window and prove the next one takes calls. Why it matters: A second gateway that has never received a call is a drawing.

cards.front: How do you approach Failover rehearsal?
cards.back: Rehearse, then put the result in the runbook. If it fails: The outage is the first test.
If the SBC and Teams offer no codec in common, the call fails, often with 488. Why it matters: Adding AMR-WB on a bypass trunk does not fix a G.711 refusal.

cards.front: How do you approach Codec intersection empty?
cards.back: Offer G.711 at minimum unless you have a measured reason not to. If it fails: The SBC allows only G.729 and the far end does not.

A-law and μ-law are both G.711. A trunk that offers the wrong one still often interoperates, and sometimes does not. Offer both if the carrier is vague. Why it matters: This is a one-line SBC change, after you have a capture.

cards.front: How do you approach G.711 law?
cards.back: Capture SDP and compare. If it fails: A new country is added and audio sounds like noise.
The words the queue plays about position or wait. A lie (‘your call is important’) is still a design choice you can decline. Why it matters: Bad messages increase abandon.

cards.front: How do you approach Comfort message?
cards.back: Say something true: whether you record, and whether you call back. If it fails: The message promises a callback the queue cannot place.

Both convenience and compliance recording require participant notification. Compliance does not ask the participant for consent in the comparison Microsoft publishes. Why it matters: A silent compliance recorder is a legal problem, not a clever config.

cards.front: How do you approach Recording disclosure?
cards.back: Confirm the partner’s announcement and test it. If it fails: Notification is off because it ‘hurt the experience.’

Know whether your recorder and your policy include emergency calls, and follow the rule you were given. Do not route emergency calls into a bot so they can be ‘handled.’ Why it matters: Emergency is a route, a location, and a carrier.

cards.front: How do you approach Do not record emergency?
cards.back: Keep the emergency voice route boring and local. If it fails: 999 matches the IVR workstream.
The case note should carry the Call-ID, the number in E.164, the queue, and the agent. Then a later complaint can be found. Why it matters: A note that says ‘called customer’ cannot be audited.

cards.front: How do you approach CRM timeline?
cards.back: Make the screen pop write those fields. If it fails: The case exists and the recording cannot be found.

A seam left on purpose for a system you might add later, using a product that already exists. It is not a promise that Microsoft will ship a feature. Why it matters: Invented roadmap items fail audits.

cards.front: How do you approach Future hook?
cards.back: Name the hook, the identifier, and the failure if you skip it. If it fails: A design depends on an unannounced SBC feature.

Older conversation says Power for the third contact-center model. The Learn article maintained on 14 October 2026 says Unify, Extend, and Connect. Why it matters: Using the old word without a mapping hides the media path.

cards.front: How do you approach Power model wording?
cards.back: Ask the vendor which of the three current models they hold. If it fails: The contract says Power and the network team opens no ports.
The list of SBCs and contact-center solutions changes. A campus page is not the list. Why it matters: Quote the list the week you buy.

cards.front: How do you approach Certified list changes?
cards.back: Link the design to the current Microsoft page and the firmware. If it fails: A purchase order cites a 2022 PDF.

In the Connect model, Microsoft’s documentation says the contact-center side does not need a phone-system license, and the Teams user who receives a transferred call does need Teams Phone and a number. Why it matters: Experts who ‘just answer in Teams’ still need a telephone.

cards.front: How do you approach User transfer license?
cards.back: License the humans who receive transfers. If it fails: The agent transfers and the expert’s client will not take the PSTN call.
A Dynamics or Teams trial proves a click path. It does not prove emergency calling, recording retention, or a busy hour. Why it matters: Pilots skip the boring gates.

cards.front: How do you approach Trial is not a design?
cards.back: Write the gates: 911, recording, overflow, certificate, rollback. If it fails: The pilot is declared production on Friday.
The numbers go back to the old route if the new path fails. If you deleted the old route, you do not have a rollback. Why it matters: Dual-running exists so rollback is a script, not a rebuild.
Keep the old trunk until the new path has a quiet week. If it fails: The maintenance window ends with no public numbers.
Call-ID, the policy you read, the ladder, and the CQD or Call Analytics row. One pack per hypothesis. Why it matters: Verbal ‘it failed’ is not a pack.

cards.front: How do you approach Evidence pack?
cards.back: Store the pack with the change ticket. If it fails: The same outage is debugged from scratch next month.
A fictional tenant name used in Microsoft samples and in this campus. It is not a customer. Why it matters: Examples use 555 numbers and example domains so nothing here is someone’s directory.

cards.front: How do you approach Contoso sample?
cards.back: Keep lab names obviously fake. If it fails: A lab script is aimed at a real tenant by find-and-replace.
Microsoft’s practice UI for what an exam looks like. It is not the product lab. Why it matters: Use it so the tool is not a surprise. Still study the skills.

cards.front: How do you approach Exam sandbox?
cards.back: Open the sandbox once before the appointment. If it fails: The first time someone sees a lab item is during the exam.

Role-based certifications expire unless you pass the free renewal on Learn. Retirement is a different event from expiry. Why it matters: A certification you earned and did not renew is not a retirement of the exam.

cards.front: How do you approach Renewal assessment?
cards.back: Calendar the renewal. Re-read what changed. If it fails: MS-700 lapses and the holder thinks the exam was retired.
When this campus and a study guide disagree, the study guide accessed the week you sit the exam wins. Why it matters: Skills move. The 27 October 2026 MS-700 update is an example.

cards.front: How do you approach Study guide wins?
cards.back: Re-open the guide before you book. If it fails: A candidate memorizes a third-party brain dump.
The device that speaks SIP to Teams and SIP or another protocol to the carrier or PBX, and enforces the edge. Why it matters: Without a certified one, Direct Routing is unsupported.

cards.front: How do you approach Session border controller?
cards.back: Pair the FQDN, not a nickname. If it fails: A router with SIP ALG is described as the SBC.
A firewall feature that rewrites SIP. It breaks Direct Routing more often than it helps. Why it matters: Microsoft’s network guidance does not want helpers in the media path.

cards.front: How do you approach SIP ALG?
cards.back: Turn SIP ALG off on the path to the proxies. If it fails: INVITEs are rewritten and the contact header points at a private address.
Teams must be able to reach the SBC. A purely private address with no public path will not pair. Why it matters: NAT without a stable signaling address is a classic failure.

cards.front: How do you approach Public IP on the SBC?
cards.back: Publish the signaling address you documented. If it fails: The SBC is only reachable on a VPN Microsoft is not on.
Proxy addresses change inside the published ranges. A firewall object built from one lookup goes stale. Why it matters: Allow the range, not the A record you saw today.

cards.front: How do you approach DNS TTL and proxies?
cards.back: Re-read the plan page when you edit the firewall. If it fails: The trunk fails after a resolver change and the certificate is blamed.
The plan page says that if you enable mutual TLS, install the Microsoft trusted roots on the SBC. Why it matters: MTLS is optional in many designs and mandatory in the way you configured.

cards.front: How do you approach Mutual TLS option?
cards.back: Match the SBC setting to what you intended. If it fails: The SBC demands a client certificate Teams is not presenting in the mode you chose.
